lesson.title: Systems of Linear Equations: Finding Where Two Lines Meet
lesson.summary: A system of linear equations asks where two lines intersect, and the elimination method turns two equations in two unknowns into the single-variable equation solving you already know, revealing the one point that satisfies both lines at once.
lesson.body:
A single linear equation, as covered earlier in this course, describes every point along one straight line. A system of linear equations puts two of these equations together and asks a sharper question: is there a point, an (x, y) pair, that satisfies both equations simultaneously. Graphically, that point is exactly where the two lines cross. If the lines have different slopes, they cross at exactly one point, and that point is the system's unique solution.

The elimination method solves a system by strategically adding or subtracting the two equations so that one variable cancels out entirely, collapsing the problem down into the single-variable equation solving from earlier in this course. Sometimes the equations are already set up to cancel a variable directly, and sometimes one or both equations first need to be multiplied by a constant so that a variable's coefficients become opposites.

Take the system 2x plus y equals 11, and x minus y equals 1. Notice that the first equation has a plus y and the second has a minus y, so simply adding the two equations together will eliminate y immediately: (2x plus x) plus (y minus y) equals 11 plus 1, which simplifies to 3x equals 12. Dividing both sides by 3, exactly the same inverse operation used on one-variable equations, gives x equals 4. With x known, substitute it back into either original equation to find y; using x minus y equals 1: 4 minus y equals 1, so y equals 3. The solution is the point (4, 3). Verify it in both original equations: 2 times 4 plus 3 is 8 plus 3, which is 11, matching the first equation, and 4 minus 3 is 1, matching the second. Both check out, confirming (4, 3) is exactly where these two lines cross.

An alternative approach, substitution, solves one equation for a single variable and plugs that expression directly into the other equation, which is often faster when a variable is already isolated or has a coefficient of 1, as x minus y equals 1 does here (x equals y plus 1, ready to substitute into the first equation). It is also worth knowing what happens when lines do not cross at a single point: if two equations describe lines with the same slope but different intercepts, the lines are parallel and the system has no solution at all, and if the two equations actually describe the exact same line, every point on that line is a solution, giving infinitely many. Recognizing these two special cases, alongside the standard single-intersection-point case worked through above, completes the picture for how two linear relationships can interact.
